purpose: Test Russian and separately identified Eastern European structures without allowing Russian, Orthodox, imperial, Soviet, émigré, Ukrainian, Polish, or Czech frames to stand in for one another.

packet_slots.position: nineteenth-century philosophy of history, Slavophile/Westernizer dispute, community, person, and sobornost
Russian religious and existential philosophy on all-unity, personhood, freedom, necessity, faith, and creative transformation
Russian literary-philosophical moral inquiry on polyphonic voice, conscience, violence/nonviolence, responsibility, and enacted life
Soviet and émigré disputes over dialectic, materialism, ideality, activity, ideology, repression, and philosophical independence
Ukrainian philosophy through Skovoroda and later reception: heart, self-knowledge, affinity or vocation, freedom, language, and contested imperial custody
Polish analytic/phenomenological and Czech phenomenological-dissident inquiry on clarity, intentional object, responsibility, care, solidarity, and living in truth

selection_rules: Russian philosophy is a historical lane, never a proxy for Eastern Europe, Slavic thought, Eurasia, or Orthodox Christianity.
Ukrainian, Polish, and Czech positions retain their own languages, institutions, political histories, and contested custody.
Literary, theological, logical, phenomenological, Marxist, and dissident genres remain distinct even when they share moral vocabulary.
Imperial, Soviet, exile, censorship, repression, and dissident conditions are mapping constraints rather than cultural essences.
No religious, nationalist, revolutionary, pacifist, or dissident position becomes Factorium guidance.
